data.title: Data Exfiltrated Over the Command and Control Channel
data.summary:
Data was removed from the environment over the same channel used to control the
compromised host. No volume, destination or content control intervened, and no alert was
raised at any point during the transfer.
data.description:
Reusing the control channel for exfiltration is the path of least resistance: it needs no
second egress route, it inherits whatever trust allowed the control channel to exist, and
it produces no new destination for a defender to notice.

That is precisely why it tends to succeed. Data loss controls are commonly scoped to
recognised channels — mail, removable media, sanctioned file sharing — and an arbitrary
outbound session to an attacker-controlled host falls outside all of them. The transfer
is then bounded only by patience.

The finding is about detection rather than about any single misconfiguration. The relevant
question for the client is what volume of data could leave over an established outbound
session before anything responded, and in this engagement the answer was that nothing did.
data.recommendation:
* Baseline outbound volume per host and alert on sustained transfers that deviate from it,
  independent of destination reputation.
* Restrict egress to a filtering proxy so that direct outbound sessions from workstations
  and servers are the exception and are visible.
* Apply data loss controls at the egress point rather than only on sanctioned applications.
* Retain flow records long enough to answer "what left, and when" after the fact.
data.short_recommendation: Baseline and alert on outbound volume; force egress through a filtering proxy.
